Parentheses can hold a brief aside or notation clarification. Fragments are occasional conversational landings, not mandatory decorations.\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua\'s no-em-dash rule governs our writing. The source\'s occasional stretched spelling, all caps, ellipses, or exclamations are observations, not a punctuation recipe. Repeated “Awesome!”, “Cool,” “That\'s it,” or “NO!” would exaggerate the surface while weakening the teaching.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Word choice and useful verbal habits\\r\\n\\r\\n### Ordinary language carries the formal idea\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source retains sufficient condition, necessary condition, contrapositive, indicator, variable, and stimulus. It gives these words a familiar handle and shows what they mean. It does not hide the vocabulary the student will need.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe conversational words are often functional: “have to,” “need,” “what happens,” “what do you know,” “the other side,” “what\'s left,” “this fits.” They describe a move the reader can make.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Word or phrase function | Source tendency | Writing instruction |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| Certainty | must, has to, necessary, no way around | Preserve the exact logical strength, then demonstrate it. |\\r\\n| Possibility | might, could, may, we don\'t know | Say what remains open and why the rule leaves it open. |\\r\\n| Drawing a consequence | so, that means, that implies, this tells me | Put the actual reason immediately before the consequence. |\\r\\n| Giving a reason | because, since | Explain the matching relationship, not merely “because that\'s the rule.” |\\r\\n| Inviting attention | let\'s look, notice, check, imagine | Name the thing to inspect or the fact to change. |\\r\\n| Naming a boundary | but, that said, sometimes, unless | Keep the qualification beside the advice it limits. |\\r\\n| Recovering context | so far, return to, now that | Remind the reader of the specific idea the new step depends on. |\\r\\n| Testing an interpretation | this fits, does that follow, what would I need | Compare the proposed meaning with the whole original sentence. |\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not replace natural speech with “identify the guaranteed outcome,” “activate the sufficient trigger,” or “execute the conditional reasoning procedure” when the learner needs an explanation. Technical wording earns its place by helping them think.\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua\'s browser corrections, 2026-10-03: define “guarantee” as the certainty supplied by the stated rule before using it to explain another idea. Explain “direction” through an actual relationship before using the word as advice. A beginner needs to see what the arrow means, which complete idea belongs on each side, and why sentence order need not match diagram order. “Read left to right” alone does not teach that. Introduce sufficient as enough and necessary as required through the example, then develop their limits.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor rule versus fact, make the hypothetical explicit: a rule tells us what would follow **if** a condition were true. It does not report that the condition happened. Contrast “Suppose this order is marked ready” with “This order is marked ready” before drawing a conclusion about an actual case. Keep the anchor sentence idiomatic and complete. Emphasis and motion around “if” should reveal that hypothetical relationship, with equally clear static information when motion is reduced.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Technical names arrive at the useful moment\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source gives a simple relationship before dissecting sufficient and necessary. It explains the contrapositive in ordinary terms before presenting the flip-and-negate shortcut. It explains why symbols help before building the first diagram. The label arrives when there is a concrete idea to attach it to.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis does not mean withholding a definition for suspense. Start with what the topic is. Then give the learner an experience that makes its vocabulary meaningful. A name should settle a distinction the reader has seen.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Small verbal irregularities create a person\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source sometimes says “little squiggle,” “little bracket cage,” “for real,” or “a bunch of different ways.” It also occasionally uses elevated words such as “ballyhoo” or “cumbersome.” This combination makes the prose human without eliminating precision.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor our material, choose the natural word for the situation. Do not manufacture slang or rare vocabulary to imitate personality. Do not import profanity, dismissive reactions, or author-specific tics. The recognizable quality should be a teacher\'s thoughtful judgment, not a checklist of eccentric phrases.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Questions that make the reader think\\r\\n\\r\\nQuestions are one of the source\'s main ways of controlling pace. They have several distinct functions. Choose the function before writing the question.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Kind of question | What the source does | What our version should do |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| **Prediction before a reveal** | Coffee/walking thought experiment asks what the reader knows, gives a blank, and says STOP. | Ask a bounded question with enough information to answer. Wait for an attempt before showing the reasoning. |\\r\\n| **One step inside a worked example** | Asks whether the sufficient condition could occur without the necessary burden. | Let the reader see the missing connection, then answer it in the walkthrough. |\\r\\n| **Meaning check** | Personalized if/then asks what the speaker knows in a proposed situation. | Read the original sentence naturally and test whether the proposed diagram preserves it. |\\r\\n| **Tempting reverse** | Tries the wrong sufficient condition and shows the interpretation failing. | Make the attractive wrong choice visible without ridiculing it. Explain the unsupported inference. |\\r\\n| **Reader objection** | FAQ voices worry about time, confidence, and whether to write. | Use the learner\'s actual objection, then explain the decision criterion. |\\r\\n| **Notation clarification** | Asks about parentheses and abbreviations. | Answer small questions where the notation first becomes relevant. |\\r\\n| **Reason for practice** | Explains why the drill asks for written contrapositives. | Say what ability the task checks and why practice may be more explicit than test-day work. |\\r\\n| **Boundary test** | Four-situation chart asks what has to happen in each case. | Compare the strongest justified answer with what could still be true. |\\r\\n\\r\\nAn exposition question can receive an immediate answer. A student question intended to train reasoning needs an actual pause. Do not ask “What do you think?” and reveal the answer in the same breath. Do not add a rhetorical question to every paragraph merely to sound interactive.\\r\\n\\r\\nA useful check has three parts: a precise prompt, a learner decision, and a reasoned explanation. For example:\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Rule:** Every blue-sticker parcel has been inspected.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> **Fact:** This parcel has been inspected.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Does the parcel have to have a blue sticker? Explain what the rule says about that direction.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe feedback should identify the gap: the rule covers blue-sticker parcels; it hasn\'t said all inspected parcels have a blue sticker. “Incorrect. Review sufficient and necessary” is too thin.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Transitions explain why the next move follows\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source\'s transitions keep the learner oriented. “So far” recovers what is established. “Let\'s return” reuses an anchor. “Now that we have a handle on” names the prerequisite for notation. “This leads me to the next question” connects a practical worry to its answer.\\r\\n\\r\\nA transition should answer one of these:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. What have we established that the next idea uses?\\r\\n2. What is still unclear?\\r\\n3. What will we change while holding the rule fixed?\\r\\n4. Why is the next representation useful now?\\r\\n\\r\\nOriginal transitions:\\r\\n\\r\\n> We know what the sticker tells us. Now let\'s see what the inspection stamp tells us.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> These sentences use different words, but they describe the same relationship. Let\'s write that relationship once.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> The arrow is pointing the right way. Check one more thing: did we keep the whole condition?\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not fill the gap with a curriculum announcement such as “Next, we will explore necessary conditions.” Say why the requirement is the next thing worth examining.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Repetition changes the reader\'s view\\r\\n\\r\\nThe breathing/air anchor appears in the opening, indicator families, contrapositive, fact chart, diagram, and target analysis. The reader keeps the same relationship while the representation changes. That saves the effort of understanding a new scenario at every turn.\\r\\n\\r\\nWithin the contrapositive explanation, the source repeats the requirement in several forms: air is needed; breathing has to have air; without air the requirement is missing; the original condition cannot hold. Each repetition supplies a step or a new angle.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor our writing, reuse an anchor while doing different work:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Read the ordinary meaning.\\r\\n2. Apply it to a case.\\r\\n3. Identify the sufficient and necessary ideas.\\r\\n4. Compare an unsupported reverse.\\r\\n5. Reword the same relationship.\\r\\n6. Show the diagram after its meaning is understood.\\r\\n\\r\\nIntroduce a fresh example for independent practice. The learner should not be able to answer only because the lesson already solved that sentence.\\r\\n\\r\\nA repeated “Keep this” slogan without new reasoning is not explanatory repetition. Nor is rendering the same instructions twice in different panels. See the demonstrated corrections in [COPY-CORRECTIONS](../wiki/COPY-CORRECTIONS.md).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Metaphor gives the reader a usable handle\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source uses doors, families, activation, burdens, brackets, and putting yourself in a condition\'s shoes. Each metaphor gives an abstract operation a physical or social handle. A small set of terms recurs, so the reader can keep using it.\\r\\n\\r\\nTransfer the method of choosing a metaphor, not the particular inventory. Prefer a familiar image that helps answer a logical question. Explain its literal meaning immediately. Remove it when it adds more things to remember than it clarifies.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor instance, a ticket can illustrate a requirement only if the rule is stated carefully. “A ticket is required to enter” does not say a ticket guarantees entry. An analogy fails if it smuggles in that reverse.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not build a competing metaphor for every sentence. Do not invent branded names for every skill. The standard technical terms remain the stable vocabulary.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Humor reduces tension without changing the rule\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source\'s coffee obsession makes an unusual absolute rule memorable. Its reluctant-student aside acknowledges the experience of being asked to guess. The imagined green checkmark gives the reader\'s desire for certainty a recognizable shape.\\r\\n\\r\\nHumor can occur inside an explanation when it makes the thought easier to understand. Joshua\'s source selection supersedes the earlier blanket restriction that wit must stay outside the explanation. It does not authorize mockery, forced slang, exaggerated praise, or an expanding comic story.\\r\\n\\r\\nUse a light aside only when it helps the reader inhabit a situation or relax around a specific mistake. Keep it optional. A paragraph should still teach clearly if the aside is removed. Do not use the source\'s distinctive jokes as templates to be copied.\\r\\n\\r\\nNever turn first-person source anecdotes into Joshua\'s biography. “I ask every student this” requires that Joshua actually does. “Students always learn better this way” requires evidence or a narrower, truthful statement.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Emphasis and visuals identify the decision\\r\\n\\r\\nBold in the source often marks the rule, an inference, a warning, or an instruction. Italics distinguish examples and sometimes emphasize a word that changes the contrast. A table lets the reader compare controlled variations. A STOP asks the reader to attempt something. A side note answers a local question without interrupting the main line for everyone.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor our material:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Bold the relationship or phrase that controls the next decision. Do not bold most of a paragraph.\\r\\n- Give an example its own space. The student should be able to find the sentence currently under discussion.\\r\\n- Put comparisons side by side when the same rule or wording is being contrasted.\\r\\n- Reveal diagram construction one meaningful step at a time. Explain each placement in English.\\r\\n- Preserve a readable text equivalent for every visual. The illustration is an explanation, not a substitute for one.\\r\\n- Make an interactive pause real. Let the learner choose when to reveal the reasoning.\\r\\n- Give a side note a specific job: answer a question, define new notation, or qualify advice. Avoid a second full lesson in a callout.\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua\'s notation correction still applies: teaching arrows should look like teaching notation, not little implementation-code boxes. Clear ordinary typography and meaningful labels should communicate the relationship.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source\'s adjusted HTML design is not a visual brand template. Our bootcamp should preserve the established Intro to LR student flow while using original visuals that serve the current concept. Student pages show the assigned work and the lesson itself; internal stage planning, assigned-start metadata, production notes, and selectable difficulty controls do not belong in the teaching prose.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The complete source progression and depth\\r\\n\\r\\nThis map records what the supplied excerpt does in order. It is not an assertion that every future lesson should cover every listed topic.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. The relationship comes before its parts\\r\\n\\r\\n**The Art of the If/Then**, HTML lines 142 to 154, opens with a plain definition, a single familiar rule, a literal interpretation, several statements of certainty, and a reason to understand the relationship beneath varied language. The transition promises to take the same example apart.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe depth comes from making “must” meaningful before presenting a list of words. The reader learns what kind of relationship they are looking for. The source also connects certainty to prior “Power Players” material, which is not included in this attachment. Our standalone introduction must supply any needed context itself.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Transfer:** first explain what a conditional says and why its direction matters. Then give a concrete example. Do not open with a diagramming task or make the definition a label attached after a quiz.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Sufficient is explained through presence and absence\\r\\n\\r\\n**The Sufficient Condition**, lines 156 to 199, contains a definition, the recurring anchor, a metaphor, the possibility that the sufficient condition does not occur, a contrast between its absence and presence, and a clarification of “activation.” It then shows **eight indicator rows with eleven displayed example forms**, all expressing the same anchor relationship, and explains why language recognition cannot replace understanding.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is more than “sufficient goes left.” The text develops what the condition does, what it does not establish, and how wording changes around it.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Transfer:** give sufficient its own explanation, contrasting cases, and nearby practice. A left-side label is useful only after “enough for what?” has a clear answer.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Necessary is developed as a requirement\\r\\n\\r\\n**The Necessary Condition**, lines 201 to 230, defines the other part, reuses the same rule, explains the requirement, and shows **ten indicator rows with eleven displayed forms**. It compares the varied wording with the sufficient-family statements and gives special attention to “only if.” It ends by explaining why symbols help isolate the relationship.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source uses the ordinary force of “necessary,” “required,” and “need” to make the technical term familiar. It does not jump directly to a memorized side rule.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Transfer:** explain what is required and why having a requirement is not the same as satisfying every condition for the result. Teach “if” and “only if” using a controlled comparison. Keep the target of each expression clear.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 4. The contrapositive is discovered before it is manipulated\\r\\n\\r\\n**The Contrapositive**, lines 234 to 285, first recovers the original relationship. It introduces a new coffee/walking thought experiment, removes the required condition, asks for a prediction, and explicitly pauses. The answer is derived from the unmet requirement. The term is then named, the original anchor revisited, and a four-situation chart sets limits on inference.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe order is important: meaning, prediction, reason, name, comparison. The flip-and-negate shortcut appears later, after the reader has a reason to believe the result.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Transfer:** preserve this order when contraposition is actually in scope. Do not rush the full procedure into the opening definition merely because it appears early in this source.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 5. Notation is introduced as a solution to varied wording\\r\\n\\r\\n**How to Diagram Conditionals**, lines 289 to 388, recovers the indicator families, explains the arrow, gives a four-step construction procedure, and builds one diagram in stages. It then explains negation, displays four original/contrapositive sign patterns, gives the shortcut, and distinguishes writing a contrapositive from reading one when needed.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe first diagram is narrated: notice the indicator, place its target, then complete the other side. Its final appearance is not used as evidence that the learner understands how to make it.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Transfer:** show each operation and its reason. Preserve Joshua\'s method and meaningful labels rather than copying the source\'s four-step count or abbreviation rule.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 6. Practical objections receive substantial answers\\r\\n\\r\\n**Quick Conditional Diagramming FAQ**, lines 390 to 433, has five questions:\\r\\n\\r\\n| Reader question | Depth of the answer | Reusable teaching value |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| When should I diagram? | Three paragraphs distinguish early training from later judgment, discuss difficult wording and chains, and address avoidance caused by uncertainty. | Give a criterion, a reason, and an honest account of the learning process. |\\r\\n| How do I know the diagram is correct? | Three paragraphs connect confidence with checked work and studying specific errors. | Teach a verification habit instead of offering confidence as a substitute for one. |\\r\\n| Does diagramming take too long? | Two paragraphs explain the proposed tradeoff and separate learning from speed. | Acknowledge the concern; explain why the slower practice step is useful now. |\\r\\n| Should I always write the contrapositive? | Two paragraphs qualify the advice. A separate note explains why the drills still require it. | Distinguish training evidence from the eventual performance habit. |\\r\\n| How should I abbreviate? | Gives a short example, a complete diagram, and advice about compact labels. | Make the notation choice purposeful and readable. Joshua\'s label guidance governs where it differs. |\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is unusually important to the overall tone. The writer gives practical uncertainty enough room to be answered. It is not squeezed into one generic reassurance.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 7. A useful shortcut is shown, then limited\\r\\n\\r\\n**Figuring Out The Language**, lines 437 to 471, defines an indicator\'s target and brackets the target in f…4050 tokens truncated…ddot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Openings, closings, and signature phrases\\r\\n\\r\\nThe mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Greeting.** \\"Hi [Name],\\" is the default (used ~519x). \\"Hey [Name],\\" for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). \\"Hello [Name],\\" (~105x) and \\"Dear [Name],\\" (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.\\r\\n- **Sign-off.** \\"Best,\\" and \\"Best regards,\\" are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). \\"Thanks,\\" when it\'s a favor or logistics (~146x). \\"Warmly,\\" / \\"Warm regards,\\" (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. \\"Talk soon,\\" (~9x) for someone he\'ll see again soon.\\r\\n- **Signature.** Almost always signed **\\"Joshua\\"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.\\r\\n- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don\'t overuse):** \\"let me know\\" (by far the most common, ~390x), \\"looking forward,\\" \\"I hope\\" / \\"hope all is well\\" / \\"hope you,\\" \\"no worries at all,\\" \\"happy to\\" / \\"more than happy to,\\" \\"just wanted to make sure,\\" \\"make sure,\\" \\"no rush,\\" \\"of course.\\"\\r\\n- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs: never.)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The apology / accountability move\\r\\n\\r\\nOne of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'m so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn\'t communicate that as well as I should have.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'ve been away from work for personal reasons, but I\'m back now and getting caught up.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Hi Sandra,\\r\\n>\\r\\n> I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Your link is the same one as before:\\r\\n> [link]\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Once again, my apologies.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Best,\\r\\n> Joshua\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** \\"I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\" The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.\\r\\n2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** \\"To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet.\\" Answer the question they actually asked. Don\'t mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.\\r\\n3. **One-sentence explanation, then \\"That is fixed now.\\"** No mechanics, no system names.\\r\\n4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, \\"pick any time it shows and it will book,\\" and the offer to do it by hand: \\"If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\"\\r\\n5. **Invite the next report:** \\"If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\"\\r\\n6. **Close with \\"Once again, my apologies.\\"** then \\"Best,\\" and \\"Joshua\\".\\r\\n\\r\\nCut from the draft, do not reuse:\\r\\n- \\"Sorry for the runaround\\" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.\\r\\n- \\"You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after.\\" Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.\\r\\n- \\"You have all 10 sessions\\" / \\"nothing was used from your package.\\" Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Situational micro-templates\\r\\n\\r\\nVerbatim-grounded reference lines for the situations that recur most. Adapt, never paste blindly.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Student reschedules / cancels:** low-pressure, no guilt.\\r\\n  > No worries at all. It happens, so please don\'t worry about it. If you would like to reschedule, just let me know.\\r\\n- **He missed / no-showed (approved make-good template):** full ownership, real reason, offer to make it right (see the apology move above). When the cause was an unexpected health issue, the approved shape is: sincerely apologize, state that a serious health scare unexpectedly took him out of commission, offer a **completely free, full LSAT session**, and hand them the complimentary booking link `https://cal.com/joshua-jtx5ud/complimentary-session`. Emphasis stays limited: bold the complimentary offer, italicize the line that one focused session can put points on the board. Draft in Gmail; never send without Joshua\'s explicit go-ahead.\\r\\n- **Consultation reminder (day-of):**\\r\\n  > Just checking in before our consultation today. Looking forward to speaking with you. I just wanted to make sure everything is still good.\\r\\n- **Consultation follow-up:** warm, specific to their situation.\\r\\n  > Really nice meeting you. I enjoyed our conversation ... I\'m glad we got to talk through where you\'re at and what you\'re aiming for on test day.\\r\\n- **Inbound prospect (hasn\'t booked):** state availability plainly, no overselling, hand them the next step.\\r\\n  > Thanks for reaching out ... I\'d be happy to talk more about what you\'re working on and see if we\'d be a good fit. You can schedule a consultation here.\\r\\n- **Student under real-life stress:** meet the person first.\\r\\n  > Please don\'t apologize ... it sounds like you are dealing with an incredibly stressful and demanding situation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The three registers\\r\\n\\r\\nWhich voice governs which surface.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Coaching (earnest) -- inbox, personal encouragement, email\\r\\n\\r\\nFully earnest. Warm, sincere, calm, patient. No jokes. The closest thing to being in the room with Joshua. Normalizes struggle, then moves to the work.\\r\\n\\r\\nReference line (target tone):\\r\\n\\r\\n> Totally normal to trip on this one. Let\'s slow down: what is the author actually concluding? Once you see it, the trap answers lose their grip. You\'ve got this.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Encouragement (student missed a hard one):** honest first, then forward. Name that it\'s genuinely hard, stay calm, move to the work. Not soft-reassuring, not cold.\\r\\n  > Missing this is expected. It\'s one of the hardest moves on the test. Let\'s slow down and see where it slipped.\\r\\n- **Accountability (student isn\'t doing the work):** gentle nudge, low pressure. Frame it as a slip, find a rhythm together. Never \\"the reps aren\'t happening,\\" never tough love.\\r\\n- **Praise (student nails it):** name the exact skill, tie it to their history, raise the bar.\\r\\n  > That\'s the cleanest you\'ve split premise from conclusion yet. Let\'s push it into the harder sets.\\r\\n- **Hard truth about the test:** state it plainly. \\"Do not expect for it to come easy. Expect to find this exhausting.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Teaching content (conversational reasoning) -- lessons, recaps, notes, drills, explanations\\r\\n\\r\\nUse [LSAT teaching voice standard](../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md), Joshua\'s selected calibration from 2026-10-02. Keep the reader beside the teacher. Explain the ordinary meaning, ground it in an original example, make the small inferences audible, ask a useful question, and show both the consequence and its limit. Introduce terminology and notation when their meaning is established. Give each concept enough development to be learned from the page.\\r\\n\\r\\nContractions and varied sentence lengths should sound natural when read aloud. Repetition should change the reader\'s view of the same relationship. Questions should give the reader actual thinking work. Light humor may appear within an explanation when it helps understanding; this supersedes the older wit-only-at-the-edges restriction. Do not force punchlines, slang, hyperbole, catchphrases, or paragraph quotas.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source governs delivery, not Joshua\'s procedure, indicator taxonomy, biography, or the scope of a lesson. Brand (sharp wit) -- landing, auth, marketing\\r\\n\\r\\nConfident and clever, the way a good lawyer is clever. Wit tied to the real skill, not wordplay for its own sake. Add to it every time a\\r\\ncorrection is made.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The rules these corrections came from\\r\\n\\r\\nThree rules already existed and all three leaked anyway, because each was\\r\\nenforced on the components that happened to exist when it was written. A surface\\r\\nadded later starts uncovered.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** [[teaching-voice]], Core voice.\\r\\n- **No internal vocabulary in student copy.** `projects/lsatu/src/features/activity-centre/CONTEXT.md`\\r\\n  carries the glossary and marks what to avoid.\\r\\n- **Every CSS token a stylesheet uses must be defined in it.** `projects/lsatu/CLAUDE.md`.\\r\\n\\r\\nGuards now live with the content rather than with each component:\\r\\n`content/instructions-voice.test.ts` checks the authored instructions, so every\\r\\nsurface that renders them is covered, including surfaces not written yet.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Corrections\\r\\n\\r\\n### Conditional opening: define the words before using them (2026-10-03)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua\'s marked browser paragraphs used “direction” and “guarantee” before making their meaning clear. The purpose paragraph also described an argument accepting more than its information supports without showing what that meant. Teach what a rule lets you conclude in plain language, then attach the vocabulary to a concrete relationship. Explain sufficient as enough and necessary as required before relying on those roles. Show what the must-arrow records and why English clause order does not determine the two sides.\\r\\n\\r\\n2026-10-03 clarification: explicitly distinguish the indicator from the complete condition it refers to. Sufficient goes left; necessary goes right. The indicator itself is not a condition in the diagram. Show the same relationship with if at the beginning and in the middle, and show necessary targets both before and after requirement language. Neither sentence position nor the words immediately following the indicator determine placement. Preserve if versus only if as different complete expressions.\\r\\n\\r\\nA rule describes what would follow **if** a condition were true; it does not say that condition happened. Bold that “if” and use meaningful in-view motion to expose the connection, with a static reduced-motion equivalent. Replace compressed ready-order wording with a natural full sentence. Give each paragraph and interaction a specific teaching job. These corrections supplement the canonical voice standard rather than adding a new writing register.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Generic reasoning prompts → concrete numbered demonstrations (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua marked four parts of the V6 opening: \\"Read each whole idea,\\" \\"Find what the statements guarantee,\\" the abstract first sentence about information, and the paragraph combining application and linking. They named goals without showing a useful action or explanation. Replace them with numbered, separate scenarios. Show the fact and rule that prove a conclusion about one case; separately show two matching rules and their new conditional conclusion. Labels should identify actual inputs or outputs. Review the whole note for repeated umbrella instructions and make task instructions executable. This follows the teaching voice: specific, concrete, short sentences, with air between distinct ideas.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Fact and rule definitions must explain the inference (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua rejected definitions that remained abstract and an explanation that did not clearly distinguish applying a rule from linking rules. Define the inputs with examples, then show the matching step and exact output. A case fact plus a rule proves something about that case. Two connecting rules produce another conditional rule without establishing a case exists. Adding a fact to the chain is a separate step. Explain all four fact situations and a hidden chain revealed by contraposition rather than leaving them implicit in an interactive model. Rules include general logical relationships, not only policies or obligations.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Boxed `L -> R` → bold teaching notation **L → R** (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua rejected the recap\'s small monospace arrow inside a pale code box. It looked like implementation text and weakened the explanation. Use a real, clearly weighted arrow in ordinary teaching typography. Explain its complete conditions before shortening them. The Some, Most, and All reference also governs the progression: introduce the whole idea, develop the individual components, then compare and combine them. A visual refresh must review that sequence, not only colors and boxes.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Concept lesson\\" → the actual reasoning title (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe recap preview exposed an internal label above the student lesson. Joshua explicitly rejected it. Use a title such as \\"Facts, Rules, and What Follows\\" and headings that teach the reasoning. Keep production labels, version metadata, and design commentary in private records. Check the rendered HTML, since its shell can introduce wording absent from the Markdown source.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Recall Rephrase Colour\\" → \\"Read, Recall, Colour\\"\\r\\nThe door\'s heading was hardcoded to a name the product does not have, one line\\r\\nunder a chip reading \\"Read, Recall, Colour\\". \\"Rephrase\\" belongs to a different\\r\\nActivity, Conditional Rephrase. A test asserted the wrong name, which is why\\r\\n2,600 passing tests never caught it.\\r\\n**Lesson:** when a test pins a string, check the string is right, not just that\\r\\nit matches.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Intake only. Nothing comes back out yet…\\" → plain instruction\\r\\nClinical and abstract, and the sentence then told her to read \\"with full\\r\\nintonation\\" while step one is silent reading. The clause that made intonation\\r\\ninternal, \\"hear it naturally in your head\\", had been dropped in an earlier edit.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a word like \\"intake\\" reads as jargon. And when copy is trimmed,\\r\\ncheck what the trimmed clause was load-bearing for.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Three beats through the stimulus\\" → \\"Three steps\\"\\r\\n\\"Beat\\" is the internal code name for one of the four method steps. The glossary\\r\\nsays students see **step**. The interface ten pixels below labelled the same four\\r\\nthings Step 1 to Step 4, so the page used two names for one thing.\\r\\n**Lesson:** never let an implementation name reach the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"22 pieces to read\\" → line removed\\r\\nA **piece** is one chunk, roughly a sentence, and the instructions on that same\\r\\npage use the word that way. The count was of stimuli, so \\"22 pieces\\" read as 22\\r\\nsentences.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a unit word must mean one thing per surface. Check what a word\\r\\nalready means on the page before reusing it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"say it back\\" → \\"tell it back\\", \\"The Read\\" → \\"The Recall\\"\\r\\nThe library door still carried both retired names. \\"The Read\\" was step four\'s\\r\\nformer name and collided with step one, which is why it was renamed.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a rename is not finished until every row carries it. The door was\\r\\nstale for months because it is a different database row from the sections.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"then a fourth\\" → \\"then a fourth step\\"\\r\\nThe noun sat three words back and the reader had to carry it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"once you have got all of it\\" → \\"once you have read all of it\\"\\r\\nAmbiguous between having read it and having remembered it, in the one clause\\r\\nthat triggers step four.\\r\\n**Lesson:** precision matters most where the sentence is an instruction.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The three-fact notice → one fact\\r\\n\\"Nothing is recording yet, the microphone opens on Start, and the section\\r\\nrecords in one take that you cannot pause.\\" Two of those are said again in step\\r\\nfour and in the long version, so she skipped the paragraph.\\r\\n**Lesson:** say it once, in the place it matters.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The method, told twice → the long version collapsed\\r\\nThe page rendered four numbered steps and then the whole written briefing saying\\r\\nthe same thing at length, both open. She read the method twice and could not\\r\\ntell which one to follow.\\r\\n**Lesson:** two explanations of one thing is worse than either alone.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"PT105.S1 · 24 stimuli · about 25 min\\" → removed\\r\\nThe section was already the second line of the title. The clock is at the foot\\r\\nand in the long version. The stimulus count measured the work in a unit she has\\r\\nno feel for.\\r\\n**Lesson:** delete a line that repeats what is above it. Do not reword it.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Booking emails: hand over the link, not the pass settings (2026-09-08)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** \\"70 minutes each, and no expiration date, so there\'s no rush to use them.\\"\\r\\n**Keep:** \\"You\'re set up on LSAT U with 10 sessions.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nSession length and expiry are admin fields. The student sees them on the booking\\r\\npage when she picks a time, so putting them in the email is detail she did not ask\\r\\nfor and has to read past to reach the link. You win a raffle. You get a bicycle. We can ask whether either condition holds in a particular case.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'A conditional statement tells us that if one condition is true, another has to be true too. It gives us a rule we can use, even before we know whether either condition is true in a particular case.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "We aren\'t saying the first condition happened. We\'re asking what would follow if it did.\\n" +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'IF\\n\' +\n      \'this condition is true\\n\' +\n      \'A case to imagine\\n\' +\n      \'THEN\\n\' +\n      \'the other condition has to be true\\n\' +\n      \'What the rule establishes\\n\' +\n      "If the first condition is true, the other must be true. Imagining that case doesn\'t tell us it happened.\\n" +\n      \'Why learn this?\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "On the LSAT, you need to distinguish what the information proves from what it leaves open. A conditional rule can help you prove a conclusion. An argument can also misuse the rule and reach a conclusion it hasn\'t proved. We\'ll practice telling those apart.\\n" +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "Let\'s read one rule.\\n" +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'If you win the raffle, you get a bicycle.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Under this rule, winning the raffle makes getting a bicycle certain. Winning without getting one would break the stated relationship. That is what we mean by a guarantee here.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Compare that with “If you win the raffle, you usually get a bicycle.” Usually allows an exception. Our rule does not. Sufficient means enough. You might not. The rule has not settled that question.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "You don\'t win the raffle. Could you still get a bicycle?\\n" +\n      \'Yes. Getting a bicycle is still possible.\\n\' +\n      \'No. Without winning, getting a bicycle is impossible.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Now suppose a fact gives us the sufficient condition. That is when we can use, or activate, the rule in its stated direction.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'You win the raffle. It is not a requirement you must satisfy before entering. The word necessary describes the relationship, not when the events occur.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "We\'re looking at the same rule from its other side. Winning is enough to establish getting a bicycle. Getting a bicycle is the result the rule requires whenever you win.\\n" +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Under our rule, what has to follow if you win?\\n\' +\n      \'You get a bicycle.\\n\' +\n      \'You ride the bicycle home.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Necessary does not mean “the next event.” It means required by this relationship. A conditional need not tell you which event caused another, or when either happened.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'You get a bicycle. Does that establish that you won the raffle?\\n\' +\n      \'Yes. Getting a bicycle proves winning.\\n\' +\n      \'No. You could get a bicycle without winning.\\n\' +\n      \'PREVIOUS LESSON\\n\' +\n      \'The sufficient condition\\n\' +\n      \'NEXT DRILL\\n\' +\n      \'Enough, required, or still open?\'\n  },\n  {\n    href: \'/dev/conditional-opening-preview?page=missing-requirement\',\n    text: \'When a requirement is missing\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Distinguish the two facts that settle something from the two that leave it open.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'What if the requirement is missing?\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Use this stated rule for a different case.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'If a report is in the published archive, it has an approval stamp.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'A report in that archive has to carry the stamp. Treat each fact as settled, not as a report that you are still waiting. Decide what it establishes before comparing the explanation.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'ONE RULE. Neither follows from this rule alone.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'The contrapositive starts from not getting a bicycle and establishes not winning the raffle. Its reasoning depends on the missing required result, not on reversing whichever words happen to appear.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'PREVIOUS DRILL\\n\' +\n      \'Same rule, different words\\n\' +\n      \'NEXT LESSON\\n\' +\n      \'Write and read the contrapositive\'\n  },\n  {\n    href: \'/dev/conditional-opening-preview?page=contrapositive\',\n    text: \'Write and read the contrapositive\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Reverse the sides, negate both complete conditions and check the meaning.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Write the meaning you already understand\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Win means you win the raffle. Get bicycle means you get a bicycle. Our original is Win → Get bicycle.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'We already know that not getting a bicycle rules out winning. Write that as ~Get bicycle → ~Win. The ~ sign means not. Not getting the outcome is different from not having received it yet.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "To write a contrapositive from a diagram, reverse the two sides and negate both complete conditions. A condition already containing not loses that not when we negate it. Let\'s try all four patterns.\\n" +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'1. NEITHER SIDE NEGATIVE\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'If you win the raffle, you get a bicycle.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'W = win the raffle. B = get a bicycle.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'W → B\\n\' +\n      \'Which is the contrapositive of W → B?\\n\' +\n      \'B → W\\n\' +\n      \'~B → ~W\\n\' +\n      \'~W → ~B\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'2. NECESSARY SIDE NEGATIVE\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'If the machine is testing, its indicator is not lit.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'T = machine is testing. L = indicator is lit.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'T → ~L\\n\' +\n      \'Which is the contrapositive of T → ~L?\\n\' +\n      \'L → ~T\\n\' +\n      \'~L → T\\n\' +\n      \'~T → L\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'3. SUFFICIENT SIDE NEGATIVE\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'If the café is not closed, its doors are unlocked.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'C = café is closed. U = doors are unlocked.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'~C → U\\n\' +\n      \'Which is the contrapositive of ~C → U?\\n\' +\n      \'U → ~C\\n\' +\n      \'C → ~U\\n\' +\n      \'~U → C\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'4. BOTH SIDES NEGATIVE\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'If an item is not marked fragile, it is not on the glass shelf.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'F = item is marked fragile. G = item is on the glass shelf.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'~F → ~G\\n\' +\n      \'Which is the contrapositive of ~F → ~G?\\n\' +\n      \'~G → ~F\\n\' +\n      \'G → F\\n\' +\n      \'F → G\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'THE COMPLETE FIVE-STEP ROUTINE\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Find the indicator. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Wall time: 0.0118 seconds\nOutput:'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '[\n  {\n    href: \'/dev/conditional-opening-preview?page=foundation-practice\',\n    text: \'DRILL\\n\' +\n      \'Enough, required, or still open?\\n\' +\n      \'Use fresh facts and build a case that exposes a reversed rule.\\n\' +\n      \'Separate the rule from the fact\\n\' +\n      \'If you win the raffle, you get a bicycle.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Start with the rule you know. Decide what the rule itself establishes before any fact arrives.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Does the rule itself tell us that you actually win the raffle?\\n\' +\n      \'Yes, it says I win.\\n\' +\n      \'No, it tells me what follows if I win.\\n\' +\n      \'Carry the ideas to new rules\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Now the situations change. Take each rule as given and decide what it establishes, what it requires and what it leaves open. A wrong answer is a reason to inspect the connection and try again.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'If it rains on Saturday, the market moves into the town hall.\\n\' +\n      "It\'s Friday. You\'ve read this rule and nothing else. Where will the market be on Saturday?\\n" +\n      \'In the town hall.\\n\' +\n      \'Outdoors, as usual.\\n\' +\n      "The rule alone doesn\'t settle it.\\n" +\n      "Saturday arrives, and it\'s raining. Now where is the market?\\n" +\n      \'In the town hall.\\n\' +\n      \'Still not settled.\\n\' +\n      \'Every student going on the museum trip has a signed permission slip.\\n\' +\n      \'Which description matches this rule?\\n\' +\n      \'Going on the trip is enough to know a student has a signed slip.\\n\' +\n      \'Having a signed slip is enough to know a student is going on the trip.\\n\' +\n      \'Each one is enough to know the other.\\n\' +\n      \'If the café runs out of bread, it closes early.\\n\' +\n      \'Today the café did not run out of bread. Did it close early?\\n\' +\n      \'No. It stayed open until the usual time.\\n\' +\n      \'Yes. It closed early.\\n\' +\n      \'Not settled. It could stay open or close early for another reason.\\n\' +\n      \'Try a fresh case\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'TRY IT\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Every delivery marked collected has a pickup receipt. What is sufficient here?\\n\' +\n      \'Marked collected\\n\' +\n      \'Has a pickup receipt\\n\' +\n      \'Test the limit with a possible case\\n\' +\n      \'Someone claims that getting a bicycle proves you won the raffle. Which possible case fits our rule but disproves that claim?\\n\' +\n      \'You win and get a bicycle.\\n\' +\n      \'You do not win, but get a bicycle as a gift.\\n\' +\n      \'You win and never get a bicycle.\\n\' +\n      \'PREVIOUS LESSON\\n\' +\n      \'The necessary condition\\n\' +\n      \'NEXT LESSON\\n\' +\n      \'Read the must arrow\'\n  },\n  {\n    href: \'/dev/conditional-opening-preview?page=must-arrow\',\n    text: \'Read the must arrow\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Put sufficient on the left and necessary on the right, wherever they appear in the sentence.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Give the relationship a shorter form\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Put the sufficient condition on the left, the necessary condition on the right, and a must arrow between them.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Sufficient: enough\\n\' +\n      \'→\\n\' +\n      \'Necessary: required\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Read the arrow as must: if the left condition is true, the right condition must be true too. It does not mean the left caused the right, or that the right happens later.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "The diagram holds the complete conditions, not the indicator word. An indicator helps you find a condition\'s job. Once you\'ve found that job, place the whole condition on its side of the arrow.\\n" +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Build the raffle diagram one step at a time\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'First find the indicator, then draw the arrow, place the complete idea it refers to, and fill the other side.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'If you win the raffle, you get a bicycle.\\n\' +\n      \'OUR DIAGRAM\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'The sentence is our starting point.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Find the indicator\\n\' +\n      \'Reset the construction\\n\' +\n      \'The sentence can move. The roles stay the same.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Compare these two versions of our raffle rule. The indicator is bold; the complete idea it refers to is in brackets.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'If [you win the raffle], you get a bicycle.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'You get a bicycle if [you win the raffle].\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'If identifies the sufficient condition in both sentences.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "In the second sentence, if appears in the middle. Its condition comes last, but winning is still enough to establish getting a bicycle. Don\'t let the first phrase in English choose the first side of your diagram.\\n" +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'You get a bicycle if you win the raffle. Which diagram preserves this sentence?\\n\' +\n      \'Get bicycle → Win\\n\' +\n      \'Win → Get bicycle\\n\' +\n      \'Recall enough and required\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Use these new examples to check the roles and their direction.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Recall card 1 of 4\\n\' +\n      \'Think before you turn\\n\' +\n      \'EXPLAIN IT IN YOUR OWN WORDS\\n\' +\n      \'Every folder marked complete contains a signed form. Which condition is enough to establish the other one?\\n\' +\n      \'Turn to the explanation\\n\' +\n      \'↻\\n\' +\n      \'Previous card\\n\' +\n      \'Revisit this card\\n\' +\n      \'Next card\\n\' +\n      \'PREVIOUS DRILL\\n\' +\n      \'Enough, required, or still open?\\n\' +\n      \'NEXT LESSON\\n\' +\n      \'Sufficient-condition words\'\n  },\n  {\n    href: \'/dev/conditional-opening-preview?page=whole-meaning\',\n    text: \'Keep the whole meaning\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Compare changed wording, keep every qualification and test what your arrow says.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Check a translation four ways\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'A diagram can point the right way and still say the wrong thing. Each check below catches a different slip in the same translation process.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Target: did you find the whole idea the indicator refers to, wherever it sits?\\n\' +\n      \'Qualification: did your short label keep every restriction?\\n\' +\n      \'Direction: did a similar-looking expression trick you into the wrong side?\\n\' +\n      \'Imagined case: does your arrow promise something the sentence leaves open?\\n\' +\n      \'Check 1: find the whole target, wherever it sits\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "An indicator\'s target is the complete word or phrase it refers to. In “All guests wearing blue badges receive vouchers,” all refers to guests wearing blue badges, not guests alone.\\n" +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "The target often comes after its indicator. But often isn\'t always. Try these sentences in order.\\n" +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'TARGET AFTER THE INDICATOR\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Only reports with editor approval are published.\\n\' +\n      \'Which complete idea does the indicator refer to?\\n\' +\n      \'reports\\n\' +\n      \'reports with editor approval\\n\' +\n      \'published\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'TARGET BEFORE THE INDICATOR\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Editor approval is necessary for publication.\\n\' +\n      \'Which complete idea does the indicator refer to?\\n\' +\n      \'publication\\n\' +\n      \'editor approval\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'THE SAME WORD CAN MOVE\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Publication makes it necessary to have editor approval.\\n\' +\n      \'Which complete idea does the indicator refer to?\\n\' +\n      \'publication\\n\' +\n      \'editor approval\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'[Having a key] is required for borrowing a locker.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Borrowing a locker requires [having a key].\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Having a key is the requirement in both sentences.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'The target comes before required in the first sentence and after requires in the second. Having a key still goes right. Neither the closest noun nor the next word is a reliable target rule. Ask which complete idea the sentence calls required, then give that idea its role.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Check 2: keep every qualification\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Once you have the target, shorten it without losing what limits it. These two sentences test the same habit from opposite sides of the arrow.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Any applicant who submits late pays a fee.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "Applicant alone isn\'t the condition. The sentence is about an applicant who submits late. Drop that restriction and your diagram makes a claim about on-time applicants too.\\n" +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Entry requires a current pass.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'A current pass is required. Has a pass drops current and would include an expired pass. A shorter label should save writing, not change the requirement.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Any applicant who submits late pays a fee. What goes left?\\n\' +\n      \'Applicant\\n\' +\n      \'Applicant submits late\\n\' +\n      \'Entry requires a current pass. What goes right?\\n\' +\n      \'Has current pass\\n\' +\n      \'Has any pass\\n\' +\n      \'Check 3: only and the only point to different targets\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Try the distinction on the raffle rule we already understand. The wording changes, but winning still tells us that you get a bicycle.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Only people who get a bicycle win this raffle.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Only refers to people who get a bicycle. Getting one is required whenever someone wins, so get a bicycle goes right.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'The only people who win this raffle are people who get a bicycle.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'The only refers to people who win. Winning is enough to establish getting a bicycle, so win the raffle goes left.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Win the raffle\\n\' +\n      \'→\\n\' +\n      \'implies\\n\' +\n      \'Get a bicycle\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Both sentences preserve the same direction. Someone who gets a bicycle as a gift without winning fits both. Neither sentence makes getting a bicycle enough to establish winning.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'TRY IT\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Only registered guests receive wristbands. What follows from receiving a wristband?\\n\' +\n      \'The person is a registered guest.\\n\' +\n      \'Nothing about registration.\\n\' +\n      \'Check 4: try the sentence from the inside\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'A Personalized If/Then lets you test what a proposed sufficient condition would establish. First read the ordinary meaning. Propose the sufficient idea. Imagine a case meeting it. Ask what the sentence now requires.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Only people wearing helmets ride the studio bikes.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'The sentence restricts riders to people wearing helmets. Keep that meaning while trying each proposed starting point.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'FIRST PROPOSED STARTING POINT\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "If I\'m riding a studio bike, what does this sentence tell me?\\n" +\n      \'I am wearing a helmet.\\n\' +\n      \'The helmet question is open.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'TRY THE OTHER STARTING POINT\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "If I\'m wearing a helmet, must I be riding a studio bike?\\n" +\n      \'Yes, the helmet proves riding.\\n\' +\n      \'No, I could wear one without riding.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'The first reading matches the sentence. The second proposed arrow fails because it rules out a case the original permits. Use the imagined situation to inspect meaning, not to supply extra facts from what usually happens.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Use the What Test beside it\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Ask a sensible question about the expression: only what? People wearing helmets. What is required? Wearing a helmet. What is enough? Riding a studio bike, under this rule, establishes that requirement.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'The What Test finds the complete target. The Personalized If/Then checks what your proposed direction says about a case. Use them together when one part of the translation is unclear.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'PREVIOUS LESSON\\n\' +\n      \'Necessary-condition words\\n\' +\n      \'NEXT DRILL\\n\' +\n      \'Same rule, different words\'\n  },\n  {\n    href: \'/dev/conditional-opening-preview?page=mixed-practice\',\n    text: \'DRILL\\n\' +\n      \'Same rule, different words\\n\' +\n      \'Mix both expression families and explain which condition belongs on each side.\\n\' +\n      \'Find the requirement, then place it\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Ask what the indicator refers to. Only what? Only if what? What is required? The target can come before or after the expression, so check its meaning in the complete sentence.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "This is the What Test. The question helps you find the indicator\'s complete target before choosing its side of the arrow. Keep any words that limit which people, objects, places, or occasions the sentence covers. The question finds the idea; the whole sentence tells you what that idea does.\\n" +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Work through the expressions below. First choose the complete target. Then place it on its side of the arrow and read the relationship in ordinary English.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'READ THE WHOLE IDEA\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'only\\n\' +\n      \'only if\\n\' +\n      \'only when\\n\' +\n      \'only where\\n\' +\n      \'always\\n\' +\n      \'requires\\n\' +\n      \'must\\n\' +\n      \'Only members are admitted.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'What is only referring to?\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Member\\n\' +\n      \'Admitted\\n\' +\n      \'From sentence to diagram\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'You have seen the expressions with help. Now use a new sentence. Identify both complete ideas, choose the sufficient one for the left, and check whether your diagram says what the sentence says.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      "If you know the meaning but hesitate over the arrow, imagine the left condition is true. Does the sentence then require the right condition? Read the whole relationship in English. If it makes a promise the original didn\'t make, change the direction.\\n" +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'BUILD THE DIAGRAM\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Only guests with a booking receive a room key.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Both complete ideas are below. Choose the sufficient condition, the one that gives you enough to establish the other. It belongs on the left of the arrow.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Receives room key\\n\' +\n      \'Guest has booking\\n\' +\n      \'Why write a diagram when I understand the sentence?\\n\' +\n      \'Check the meaning, not just the word\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'TRY IT\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'A student graduates only if the project is completed. Which is the same rule?\\n\' +\n      \'If the student graduates, the project was completed.\\n\' +\n      \'If the project is completed, the student graduates.\\n\' +\n      \'More sentences to recall and explain\\n\' +\n      \'Mix both families without the label\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'These sentences mix both kinds of expression, and nothing tells you which kind is coming. For each one, find the complete idea the expression refers to. Then decide which idea is enough and put it on the left. Check your translation before moving on.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'SENTENCE 1 OF 6\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'The match moves indoors if the forecast shows lightning.\\n\' +\n      \'What does if refer to? Choose the complete idea.\\n\' +\n      \'the forecast shows lightning\\n\' +\n      \'the forecast\\n\' +\n      \'the match moves indoors\\n\' +\n      \'Which complete idea goes on the left of the must arrow?\\n\' +\n      \'Match moves indoors\\n\' +\n      \'Forecast shows lightning\\n\' +\n      \'Check sentence 1\\n\' +\n      \'Try sentence 1 again\\n\' +\n      \'Previous mixed sentence\\n\' +\n      \'Next mixed sentence\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Moving between sentences keeps your choices and feedback.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Keep the rule while the wording changes\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'You now know both groups. Set the group names aside and read what each sentence promises.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'KEEP THIS ORIGINAL RULE\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Every envelope in the dispatch tray is stamped.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'An envelope in the tray has to be stamped. A stamped envelope could still be elsewhere. Use that possible case to check each new version.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Version 1\\n\' +\n      \'Version 2\\n\' +\n      \'Version 3\\n\' +\n      \'Version 4\\n\' +\n      \'Only stamped envelopes go into the dispatch tray.\\n\' +\n      \'Does this preserve the original rule, or reverse it?\\n\' +\n      \'Same rule\\n\' +\n      \'Reversed rule\\n\' +\n      \'PREVIOUS LESSON\\n\' +\n      \'Keep the whole meaning\\n\' +\n      \'NEXT LESSON\\n\' +\n      \'When a requirement is missing\'\n  },\n  {\n    href: \'/dev/conditional-opening-preview?page=contrapositive-practice\',\n    text: \'DRILL\\n\' +\n      \'Put the whole process together\\n\' +\n      \'Build an original diagram and its contrapositive for six fresh sentences.\\n\' +\n      \'Build an original and its contrapositive\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'For each sentence, identify the indicator and both complete conditions. Choose the original diagram, then its contrapositive. Read both back before checking. If an answer needs revision, inspect the direction, qualifications and negation, then retry.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'SENTENCE 1 OF 6\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'01\\n\' +\n      \'If a parcel has a red tracking tag, its sender has paid for tracking.\\n\' +\n      \'RT\\n\' +\n      \'Parcel has red tracking tag\\n\' +\n      \'PT\\n\' +\n      \'Sender has paid for tracking\\n\' +\n      \'Original diagram for item 1\\n\' +\n      \'PT → RT\\n\' +\n      \'RT → PT\\n\' +\n      \'~RT → ~PT\\n\' +\n      \'Contrapositive for item 1\\n\' +\n      \'PT → RT\\n\' +\n      \'~RT → ~PT\\n\' +\n      \'~PT → ~RT\\n\' +\n      \'Check both diagrams\\n\' +\n      \'Try item 1 again\\n\' +\n      \'Previous sentence\\n\' +\n      \'Next sentence\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'Moving between sentences keeps your choices and feedback.\\n\' +\n      \'\\n\' +\n      \'PREVIOUS LESSON\\n\' +\n      \'Write and read the contrapositive\\n\' +\n      \'Return to lessons\'\n  }\n]'}]
